summary: Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) used for major depression and sometimes for sleep and smoking cessation support. Effective for some people when SSRIs don’t work, but comes with real risks: heart rhythm problems, strong anticholinergic side effects, and dangerous overdose toxicity.
description: Nortriptyline is an older antidepressant (a tricyclic) that can help with mood, anxiety that rides along with depression, and sometimes sleep—especially when taken at bedtime. It’s not a “light” medication: it can cause dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, and heart rhythm changes, and it’s one of the more dangerous antidepressants in overdose. It also carries the standard antidepressant warning about increased suicidal thoughts/behaviors in younger patients. If you use it, you use it intentionally: start low, go slow, and monitor closely.
patient_summary: Nortriptyline is an older antidepressant (a tricyclic) that can help with mood and sometimes sleep—especially when taken at bedtime. It’s not a “light” medication: dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, and heart rhythm changes are common, and overdose can be dangerous. It also carries the antidepressant suicidality warning in younger patients. Start low, go slow, and don’t change the dose without your prescriber.

primary.context: An alternative antidepressant option for unipolar depression, especially when first-line options aren’t effective or tolerated. Usually taken at bedtime to improve tolerability.

off_label.context: Sometimes used at low bedtime doses when depression/anxiety is tangled up with poor sleep. Not a dedicated sleep medication, but the bedtime dosing and antihistamine-like effects can help some people.
May be used with behavioral support as an alternative/adjunct for smoking cessation in select cases, started at least 2 weeks before a planned quit date.

therapeutic_response.display: Depression: early effects often 1-2 weeks; fuller response typically 4-6 weeks

common_adverse_effects.effect: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary hesitancy, blurred vision)
common_adverse_effects.notes: This is the TCA signature. Dry mouth and constipation are the usual headline. Constipation can become severe—hydrate, fiber, movement, and talk to your clinician early rather than later.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Common (especially early and in older adults)
common_adverse_effects.notes: Standing up too fast can make you lightheaded. It can show up in the first week and stick around. Move slower, hydrate, and report fainting or near-fainting.
Some people feel sleepy; others just feel ‘slower’ for a bit. Bedtime dosing often improves tolerability. If you feel unsafe to drive, don’t drive.
Nortriptyline can increase heart rate and affect conduction. New palpitations, chest pain, fainting, or severe dizziness need prompt evaluation.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: More likely in older adults or at higher doses
common_adverse_effects.notes: If you feel confused, disoriented, or ‘not yourself,’ that’s not a side effect to ignore—especially in older adults.

serious_risks.risk: Cardiac conduction abnormalities and life-threatening arrhythmias (risk increases with overdose, preexisting conduction disease, and higher doses)
Seizures (especially in overdose or in patients with seizure vulnerability)
Serotonin syndrome (especially with other serotonergic agents; can include agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, muscle rigidity, high fever)
Severe urinary retention or paralytic ileus (medical emergency risk)
Acute angle-closure glaucoma (eye pain, redness, vision changes—emergency)
Hyponatremia/SIADH (rare; higher risk in older adults—confusion, weakness, headache)
Mania/hypomania or severe agitation (especially if bipolar disorder is present)

safety.black_box_warning: Suicidality in children, adolescents, and young adults: Antidepressants increased the risk compared with placebo of suicidal thinking and behavior (suicidality) in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies of major depressive disorder (MDD) and other psychiatric disorders. Anyone considering the use of nortriptyline or any other antidepressant in a child, adolescent, or young adult must balance this risk with the clinical need. Appropriately monitor patients of all ages who are started on antidepressant therapy and observe them closely for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual changes in behavior. Advise families and caregivers of the need for close observation and communication with the health care provider. Nortriptyline is not approved for use in pediatric patients.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to nortriptyline or related dibenzazepines, or any component of the formulation
Use during the acute recovery phase after myocardial infarction
Concomitant use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or use within 14 days of stopping nortriptyline or the MAOI
Initiation of nortriptyline in a patient receiving IV methylene blue
High risk of dangerous arrhythmia in patients with known serious conduction disease (relative contraindication; requires specialist-level caution)

precautions: Cardiac conduction and rhythm risk: TCAs can prolong PR/QRS/QT and may trigger serious arrhythmias—risk rises with higher doses, overdose, and preexisting heart disease or conduction disorders
Overdose toxicity: Tricyclic antidepressants are among the most dangerous antidepressants in overdose (life-threatening arrhythmias, seizures, coma)
Serotonin syndrome risk: Especially when combined with other serotonergic drugs; can be severe and rapid-onset
Anticholinergic burden: Constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, confusion—higher risk in older adults and at higher doses
Orthostatic hypotension and falls: Dizziness/syncope can happen, especially early and in older adults
Mania/hypomania switch: Can precipitate mania in bipolar disorder—screen before starting and avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder
Angle-closure glaucoma risk in susceptible individuals due to pupil dilation/anticholinergic effects
Do not combine with MAOIs (or within 14 days): serious interaction risk

interactions.interactant: MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid, selegiline; also IV methylene blue)
interactions.mechanism: Contraindicated: serious interaction risk (including serotonin toxicity and dangerous blood pressure/neurologic effects).
interactions.action: Do not combine. Allow 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting nortriptyline, and 14 days between stopping nortriptyline and starting an MAOI.

interactions.interactant: Other serotonergic agents (SSRIs/SNRIs, tramadol, linezolid, triptans, St. John’s wort, certain opioids)
interactions.mechanism: Serotonin syndrome risk increases when multiple serotonergic drugs are combined.
interactions.action: Use caution, monitor closely for serotonin syndrome symptoms (agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, muscle rigidity, fever). Seek urgent care for severe symptoms.

interactions.interactant: CYP2D6 inhibitors (examples: fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion; some antipsychotics)
interactions.mechanism: Can increase nortriptyline levels and side effects (anticholinergic effects, sedation, cardiac effects).
interactions.action: Dose adjustments and/or therapeutic drug monitoring may be needed. Report side effects early.

interactions.interactant: QT-prolonging medications or other arrhythmia-risk meds
interactions.mechanism: Additive risk for QT prolongation and arrhythmias.
interactions.action: Avoid high-risk combinations when possible and consider ECG monitoring in at-risk patients.

interactions.mechanism: Additive sedation, dizziness, impaired coordination; higher fall risk.
interactions.action: Avoid or minimize. If combined, use extreme caution with driving and activities requiring alertness.

interactions.interactant: Anticholinergic medications (diphenhydramine, benztropine, oxybutynin, many sleep aids)
interactions.mechanism: Anticholinergic burden skyrockets: constipation, urinary retention, confusion, blurred vision, falls.
interactions.action: Avoid stacking anticholinergics when possible—especially in older adults.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Suicidality and clinical worsening: monitor all ages, especially <25 and during the first 1-2 months or dose changes (watch for agitation, insomnia, irritability, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania/mania).

Cardiac monitoring: heart rate, blood pressure, and ECG in older adults and in patients with preexisting cardiac disease or conduction risk; reassess if palpitations, syncope, or chest symptoms occur.
Orthostatic vitals: monitor for dizziness/syncope, especially early and after dose increases.
Anticholinergic effects: constipation severity, urinary retention symptoms, blurred vision, confusion—especially in older adults and those on other anticholinergics.
Serum sodium in at-risk populations (older adults, diuretic use, low baseline sodium, severe medical illness), particularly during initiation and dose changes.
Blood glucose in patients with diabetes or metabolic risk; monitor adherence and overall stability since mood symptoms can impact diabetes management.
Therapeutic drug monitoring when clinically indicated: draw a trough level just before the next dose; typical therapeutic range 50 to 170 ng/mL; laboratory alert level around 300 ng/mL.
Functional outcomes: sleep quality, daytime alertness, ability to work/school, and overall impairment—because “less depressed” isn’t enough if the medication makes life unlivable.

special_populations.pregnancy: Nortriptyline crosses the placenta and may have altered clearance during pregnancy (CYP2D6 activity can increase, especially in the third trimester), meaning dose adjustments may be needed. Therapeutic drug monitoring is often recommended monthly during pregnancy and again 2 to 6 weeks postpartum to avoid toxicity while maintaining efficacy. Untreated depression also carries pregnancy risks (preterm birth, low birth weight, preeclampsia, postpartum depression), so the decision is not simply “meds or no meds.” TCAs are generally not first-line for treatment-naïve pregnant patients, but nortriptyline may be considered as an alternative when other options are ineffective or contraindicated, using the lowest effective dose of a single agent whenever possible.
special_populations.lactation: Nortriptyline is present in breast milk. Available data suggest relatively low infant exposure (reported relative infant dose around 1.3% in one case report) and adverse events have not been consistently observed. Even so, infants should be monitored for sedation and poor feeding. If starting a new antidepressant in a treatment-naïve breastfeeding patient, other agents are often preferred; however, nortriptyline may be a preferred TCA if a TCA is needed.
special_populations.pediatric: Nortriptyline is not approved for pediatric patients. Antidepressants carry an increased risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies. Controlled trials have not shown TCAs to be superior to placebo for pediatric depression, and SSRIs are typically first-line. Nortriptyline may be considered only in select cases after other options fail and when comorbid conditions influence the decision, with close monitoring.
special_populations.geriatric: Avoid when possible. Nortriptyline is identified as potentially inappropriate in adults ≥65 due to strong anticholinergic effects and risk of sedation and orthostatic hypotension, with higher risks for falls, confusion, and hyponatremia/SIADH. If used despite this, start very low, titrate slowly, consider ECG and sodium monitoring, and reassess frequently.
special_populations.renal_impairment: No dosage adjustment is typically required, including in dialysis settings, but use with caution due to variability in clearance and increased sensitivity to anticholinergic and QT-prolonging effects in dialysis patients.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Metabolized hepatically; use with caution. Many experts reduce initial and maintenance doses by ~50% in hepatic impairment with cautious titration based on response and tolerability, especially given the narrow therapeutic index.

pharmacokinetics.half_life: 14 to 51 hours (mean ~26 hours); longer in older adults (mean ~45 hours reported)
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic, extensive first-pass; CYP2D6 is the major pathway (CYP1A2/CYP2C19/CYP3A4 minor)
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine (mostly as metabolites; small amounts unchanged)
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: May be taken without regard to food (practical dosing guidance)

dosing.titration: Nortriptyline dosing is usually bedtime-based for tolerability. The goal is the lowest effective dose that improves mood without causing intolerable anticholinergic or cardiac side effects. Some people need therapeutic drug monitoring when response or side effects don’t match the dose.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Nortriptyline should usually be tapered—not stopped abruptly—especially after you’ve been on it for 4 weeks or longer. Tapering helps reduce withdrawal symptoms and makes it easier to tell the difference between discontinuation effects and depression returning.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Nortriptyline (Pamelor) is a tricyclic antidepressant used to treat {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:major depressive disorder}. In psychiatry, it’s usually considered an alternative option—often when first-line antidepressants weren’t a fit, or when a clinician is intentionally choosing a TCA based on your symptoms and history.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (Unipolar)}: Depressed mood, loss of interest, sleep/appetite changes, low energy, poor concentration
Depression with prominent sleep disruption: Often dosed at bedtime to reduce daytime side effects and support sleep continuity
Smoking cessation support (alternative/adjunct): Used with behavioral support in select cases when other options aren’t tolerated
off_label: Insomnia related to depression/anxiety (low-dose bedtime use in select patients)
ADHD (limited data; not a routine option and usually reserved for complex cases)

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: I felt kind of dry and sluggish at first—like my body was protesting.
The first few nights I slept heavier… but waking up was rough.
It didn’t change my mood overnight, but it took the edge off the doom-spiral.
It wasn’t happiness—more like the floor stopped dropping out.
I started doing things again without forcing every step.
My brain got a little quieter. Less rumination, less looping.
items.note: Early improvement can show up in 1-2 weeks, but fuller benefit often takes 4-6 weeks at a therapeutic dose.

quotes: My mouth was so dry I carried water everywhere.
Constipation became a whole new hobby I didn’t ask for.
Standing up too fast made me see stars.
items.note: Dry mouth, constipation, and dizziness/orthostatic symptoms are common and dose-related.

quotes: I wasn’t knocked out, but I felt a little dulled for a while.
My brain felt slower in the morning until we adjusted the dose timing.
Once we got the dose right, I felt more steady than sleepy.
items.note: Nortriptyline is often less sedating than some other TCAs, but sedation and cognitive slowing can still happen—especially early or at higher doses.

items.category: When It’s Not the Right Fit
quotes: It helped my mood, but my heart felt weird—like it was racing.
The side effects weren’t worth it for me.
I got more agitated and wired, which was the opposite of what I needed.
items.note: New palpitations, fainting, severe dizziness, confusion, or agitation are not “push through it” symptoms—those are check-in-now symptoms.

sections.intro: Real talk: nortriptyline can be a solid med for the right person, but it has a “TCA personality.” Here’s what people commonly report:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Nortriptyline isn’t a quick-hit medication. It builds. You might feel side effects early, while the antidepressant benefit takes longer to show up.
key_points: First dose: Some people notice dry mouth, mild sedation, dizziness, or GI changes quickly
1-2 weeks: Early depression improvement may start (sleep, appetite, energy can shift first)
4-6 weeks: Typical window for fuller antidepressant response at a therapeutic dose
4-9 hours: Time to peak blood levels after a dose
14-51 hours: Half-life (average around 26 hours; can be longer in older adults)

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Nortriptyline can be very effective for some people with major depression—especially when other antidepressants didn’t land well. The catch is the timeline: you usually need a real trial (weeks, not days), and you often need dose adjustments based on both symptoms and tolerability. If it’s going to work, you often see the first signs within 1 to 2 weeks, with continued gains through weeks 4 to 6.
sections.value: Early changes in 1-2 weeks; fuller effect in 4-6 weeks
sections.clinical_details: Response varies widely. A practical assessment window is a consistent therapeutic dose for several weeks, with close monitoring for side effects and safety issues (especially cardiac and anticholinergic effects). Therapeutic drug monitoring can help confirm whether blood levels are in a typical effective range when response is unclear or side effects are significant.

patient_counseling: If you’re under 25, or you’re starting/changing dose: you (and your people) watch closely for worsening depression, agitation, impulsivity, insomnia, or suicidal thoughts—especially in the first 1-2 months.

If constipation, urinary retention, severe dry mouth, confusion, or blurry vision becomes intense—don’t “power through.” That’s a dose/tolerability conversation.
Avoid alcohol and sedating meds unless your prescriber explicitly okays the combo.
Don’t stop abruptly after you’ve been on it a few weeks—tapering matters.
An FDA Medication Guide is required to be dispensed with this medication.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision), dizziness/orthostatic symptoms, and fatigue or sedation (varies). Nortriptyline is often less sedating than some other TCAs, but side effects are still dose-related and real.

sections.intro: Nortriptyline has meaningful interaction risk because it affects serotonin/norepinephrine systems, has anticholinergic properties, and is metabolized mainly by CYP2D6. Translation: some combinations can raise blood levels, increase side effects, or raise cardiac risk.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Nortriptyline should usually be tapered—not stopped abruptly—especially after you’ve been on it for 4 weeks or longer. Tapering helps reduce withdrawal symptoms and makes it easier to tell the difference between discontinuation effects and depression returning.
key_points: If treatment lasted ≥4 weeks: common approach is tapering over 2 to 4 weeks (longer if high dose, long duration, or prior withdrawal problems).
If treatment lasted 2 to 3 weeks: taper over 1 to 2 weeks is often reasonable.
<2 weeks of treatment: tapering may not be necessary, but individualized judgment still matters.
Withdrawal symptoms can include: lethargy, headache, sweating, tremor, irritability, anxiety, agitation, low mood, insomnia/vivid dreams, and GI upset.
If withdrawal becomes intolerable: resume the previous dose and taper more slowly.
Long-term treatment (>6 months): some patients do best with a very slow taper (weeks to months; select cases may require >3 months).
Switching with MAOIs: allow 14 days between discontinuing nortriptyline and starting an MAOI, and 14 days between discontinuing an MAOI and starting nortriptyline.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Nortriptyline dosing is usually bedtime-based for tolerability. The goal is the lowest effective dose that improves mood without causing intolerable anticholinergic or cardiac side effects. Some people need therapeutic drug monitoring when response or side effects don’t match the dose.

adult.depression_initial: 25 to 50 mg PO once daily at bedtime (some experts start 25 mg QHS for most patients to improve tolerability; sensitive patients may start as low as 10 mg daily)
adult.depression_titration: Increase by 25 to 50 mg/day at intervals ≥1 week based on response and tolerability (more rapid titration may be used only in closely supervised settings)
adult.depression_typical: 50 to 150 mg/day (often once daily at bedtime; may divide if needed for tolerability)
adult.depression_max: 150 mg/day (some patients may tolerate and benefit from up to 200 mg/day with careful monitoring)
adult.sleep_initial: 10 to 25 mg PO at bedtime (low-dose bedtime use may help sleep when insomnia is linked with depression/anxiety; not a standalone insomnia medication)
adult.smoking_cessation_initiation: Start ≥2 weeks before quit date: Days 1-3: 25 mg QHS; Days 4-7: 50 mg QHS; Day 8 and later: 75 mg QHS (some patients divide dosing 2-3 times/day for tolerability; may titrate up to 125 mg/day if needed to reduce cravings)
adult.renal: No dosage adjustment necessary for any degree of kidney dysfunction in most cases; use caution due to variability in clearance and increased sensitivity in dialysis patients
adult.hepatic: No formal manufacturer adjustment; many experts reduce initial and maintenance doses by ~50% in hepatic impairment and titrate cautiously
adult.geriatrics: Avoid use when possible (Beers Criteria). If used, start 10 to 25 mg/day and titrate slowly with close monitoring for anticholinergic effects, orthostasis, and cardiac effects

sections.simple_explanation: This is a slow-build medication. Side effects can show up early, while the antidepressant benefit often takes weeks. Bedtime dosing helps many people tolerate it. If the dose goes up and you feel worse (confused, faint, heart racing, severe constipation), that’s not “just adjustment”—that’s reassessment.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Nortriptyline can be used in specific scenarios during pregnancy and breastfeeding, but it’s not usually the first medication chosen for someone starting treatment from scratch. Decisions should be shared and individualized, balancing relapse risk with medication risk. Older adults are a high-risk group due to anticholinergic effects and falls.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Nortriptyline is available in capsules and an oral solution. Most people take it once daily, often at bedtime.
items: Capsule (oral): 10 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg, 75 mg (generic available)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Nortriptyline works mainly by increasing norepinephrine (and to a lesser extent serotonin) signaling in the brain by blocking reuptake. It also hits other receptors—histamine and muscarinic (anticholinergic) receptors—which is why you can see side effects like dry mouth, constipation, sedation, blurred vision, and dizziness. The antidepressant effect builds over time and likely involves longer-term receptor and signaling changes, not just immediate neurotransmitter changes.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Nortriptyline is usually not a first-choice antidepressant today because TCAs have more side effects and higher overdose danger than SSRIs/SNRIs. But it still has a real role: it can be effective for unipolar depression when first-line options fail or aren’t tolerated, and it’s sometimes chosen when a clinician wants a more norepinephrine-forward antidepressant. Bedtime dosing can help people who struggle with sleep during depression, but it’s not a clean insomnia medication. It requires intentional prescribing: screening for bipolar disorder, checking cardiac risk, cautious titration, and close monitoring—especially early and in older adults.

faqs.q: What is nortriptyline used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: Nortriptyline is used to treat unipolar major depressive disorder. In real-world psychiatry, it’s often an alternative option when first-line antidepressants (like SSRIs/SNRIs) weren’t effective or weren’t tolerated. It’s sometimes used at low bedtime doses when depression and anxiety are tangled up with poor sleep, but it’s not a dedicated sleep medication.

faqs.q: How long does nortriptyline take to work?
faqs.a: Some people notice early changes in 1 to 2 weeks, but fuller antidepressant benefit typically builds over 4 to 6 weeks at a therapeutic dose. Side effects can show up earlier than the mood benefit, which is why slow titration matters.

faqs.q: Why is nortriptyline usually taken at bedtime?
faqs.a: Bedtime dosing often improves tolerability. It can reduce daytime dizziness or sedation, and for some people it supports sleep continuity. It also helps keep the routine simple for a medication that’s usually taken once daily.

faqs.q: Is nortriptyline safe for children or teens?
faqs.a: Nortriptyline is not approved for pediatric patients. Antidepressants carry an increased risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies. If a clinician ever considers it in a younger patient, it should be a careful, specialist-level decision with close monitoring and family/caregiver involvement.

In short-term studies, antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults (typically 18 to 24). In adults over 24, that short-term increased risk wasn’t seen, and in adults 65 and older a reduced risk was observed. Regardless of age, anyone starting or changing dose should be monitored closely for worsening depression, agitation, impulsivity, insomnia, or suicidal thoughts—especially in the first 1 to 2 months.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: The big ones are anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary hesitancy), dizziness or feeling faint when standing up (orthostatic hypotension), and fatigue or sedation (variable). Palpitations can occur, and cognitive effects (confusion) are more likely in older adults or at higher doses.

Yes. Tricyclic antidepressants are among the most dangerous antidepressants in overdose because they can cause life-threatening heart rhythm problems and seizures. If overdose is possible or safety is a concern, clinicians often choose a different antidepressant with a safer overdose profile.

faqs.q: What medications should not be mixed with nortriptyline?
faqs.a: MAOIs are a hard no (and you need a 14-day gap in either direction). Caution is also needed with other serotonergic drugs (serotonin syndrome risk), strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (can raise nortriptyline levels), QT-prolonging medications (cardiac risk), alcohol and sedatives (more dizziness/sedation), and other anticholinergics (side effects stack fast).

faqs.q: Do I need blood levels or an ECG?
faqs.a: Sometimes. ECG monitoring is common in older adults and in anyone with cardiac history or symptoms like palpitations or fainting. Blood levels (therapeutic drug monitoring) can be useful when response is unclear, side effects are significant, doses are higher, or interactions could be raising levels. Typical trough therapeutic range is often cited as 50 to 170 ng/mL.

faqs.q: How do I stop nortriptyline safely?
faqs.a: If you’ve been on it for 4 weeks or longer, tapering over 2 to 4 weeks is a common approach, but longer tapers are often needed after long-term use or at higher doses. If withdrawal symptoms are rough, the usual move is to go back to the previous dose and taper more slowly. Don’t do abrupt stops unless your prescriber tells you to for a safety reason.

faqs.q: Is nortriptyline okay in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: It can be used in select situations, but it’s usually not the first choice for someone starting treatment for the first time during pregnancy or while breastfeeding. Pregnancy can change how the body clears nortriptyline (especially later in pregnancy), so monitoring and dose adjustments may be needed. In breastfeeding, infant exposure appears low in available reports, but infants should be monitored for sedation or poor feeding. Decisions should be individualized and shared with your clinician.

seo.title: Nortriptyline (Pamelor): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects, and Safety Warnings
seo.description: Nortriptyline (Pamelor) is a tricyclic antidepressant used for major depression and sometimes for sleep or smoking cessation support. Learn dosing, side effects (dry mouth, constipation, dizziness), cardiac risks, suicidality warning, interactions, and tapering.
